1:
Who was actually summoned is a question of two phrases, and Ellicott separates them. If the elders of Israel are to be distinguished from the heads of the tribes rather than identified with them, as the old Greek version does, then the first expression probably refers to the chiefs of official rank, such as the princes and the counsellors of the king, and the second to the feudal chiefs of the great families of the various tribes. These alone were specially summoned; but since the dedication festival was blended with the Feast of Tabernacles, all the men of Israel naturally assembled at Jerusalem without any summons at all. Gill hesitates over the same word from the other side, taking the elders for the judges in the several cities or, as others say, the senators of the great sanhedrim, though he adds that it is a question whether as yet there was such a court. Keil and Delitzsch stand back from the detail and set out the shape of the whole: the transaction consisted of three parts and the chapter arranges itself in three sections accordingly, the conveyance of the ark and the tabernacle into the temple with the words Solomon spoke, the dedicatory prayer, and the blessing of the congregation with the sacrifices and the feast.

Why the dedication came so long after the building is answered by Clarke from the calendar. Solomon deferred it to the year after the temple was finished, he says, because that year was a jubilee — the ninth, on the reckoning of the archbishop whose annals he follows, opening the fourth millenary of the world. He then lays the fortnight out day by day: the eighth of the seventh month was the first of the seven days of dedication, the tenth was the fast of expiation on which the jubilee was proclaimed by sound of trumpet, the fifteenth began the feast of tabernacles, and on the day after the twenty-second the people returned home. Ellicott gives the same interval more briefly, that the festival was deferred for nearly a year after the completion of the temple, and notes that on this occasion it was doubled in duration, from seven days to fourteen.
2:
What the name Ethanim signifies divides the two witnesses who take it up. Keil and Delitzsch canvass three derivations and keep the first: one scholar renders it flowing brooks, a second supposes it denotes the equinox, which the plural form by no means favours, and a third, placing this seventh division of the year between mid-September and mid-October, renders it gifts. They answer that the period intended falls rather between the new moon of October and that of November, when the rainy season commences in Palestine, so that the title may very well derive from brooks running constantly again. Ellicott adopts the rejected derivation: the interval, he says, ran from late September into early October, and the word means gifts, since it brought with it the vintage and the last of the crops; from the old Targum he adds that this once opened the civil year, as Abib opened the ecclesiastical, and he notes that on this occasion the observance was doubled in length, running fourteen days instead of seven.

Which festival was being kept is a further disagreement, and here Gill stands against the rest. Clarke says flatly that Tabernacles is meant, celebrated in the seventh division of the ecclesiastical year, and does not argue the point; Ellicott calls it the most joyful solemnity Israel had, marking the harvest of every fruit the land bore and commemorating their old life under tents in the wilderness, and judges it peculiarly fitting that the moving of the ark from a portable shrine into a fixed and splendid habitation should receive that higher consecration. Gill denies the identification outright. Tabernacles began on the fifteenth and ran a week, he grants, and fell within these very days; but what is named here must be the dedication of the temple, kept earlier, since the pair together occupied a fortnight and the crowd was dismissed on the twenty-third. He also describes who made up that crowd: not the summoned dignitaries only, but common people in great numbers, come to watch the ark carried in and the house consecrated, and readier to come because within days every male in Israel was due to appear there anyway.
3:
Who was entitled to carry the ark is settled by Ellicott from the distribution of offices, and he finds the narrative exact about it. Bearing it on its journeys belonged properly to the Levites of the family of Kohath, but taking it out of the Holy of Holies, or from whatever answered to that in the tent erected on Zion, and replacing it there, was work for the priests alone. Hence the sequence of the account is literally accurate: first the priests take up the ark, then priests and Levites together bring up the holy things, and lastly the priests carry it into the oracle. He adds that Josephus goes further and declares that on so solemn an occasion the priests themselves bore it, as at the passage of the Jordan and the circuit round Jericho, the Levites carrying only the vessels and furniture.

Henry reaches the same conclusion from the other end, by asking why the wilderness arrangement had differed. There the Levites carried it because at that time there were not enough priests to do so; here, this being its last journey, the priests took it up themselves, as they had been ordered to do at Jericho. Keil and Delitzsch treat the clause about the Levites as a supplementary notice rather than a second act, introduced according to the general diffuseness of early Hebrew narrative in order to state more precisely who brought up the sacred vessels.

Which tent was meant is the one point on which the witnesses divide. That same pair are definite: the tent of meeting named here is not the shelter erected on Zion, which can be shown never to have borne the title and which another account expressly distinguishes from it, but the Mosaic tabernacle at Gibeon, before which Solomon had earlier sacrificed. Clarke reports both and declines to choose. It is generally agreed, he says, that two stood at the time, one at Gibeon and the other in the city of David, the latter constructed as a temporary residence against the day a house should be built; which of them was taken into the temple is not well known, and some think both were, to prevent any danger of idolatry, though he should rather suppose the Gibeon one was brought in and the makeshift demolished.

Ellicott takes the practical view that the question need not be decided, since probably every section of the ministering families brought up in solemn procession whatever had been entrusted to it. By the order of the law the Kohathites had charge on the march of the ark and the vessels, the Gershonites of the hangings, and the Merarites of the boards and pillars and the outer court; that order, he judges, was no doubt followed as far as possible on this last occasion. What became of the older structure and its furniture, so far as it was now disused, we are not told, but all was probably laid up as a sacred relic of antiquity somewhere within the precincts — which, he notes, seems implied in the famous tradition that the prophet was enabled to hide by miracle the tabernacle, the ark and the altar of incense when the house was destroyed.
5:
Where the innumerable sacrifice was offered is placed by two witnesses at slightly different moments. Ellicott sets it beside an older precedent, the ceremonial of the day when David brought up the ark to Zion, where the bearers went six paces and he sacrificed oxen and fatlings; the inaugural offering corresponded to that on a grand scale, and was made before the ark, either as it left Zion or on arrival, before it passed out of sight into the oracle. Keil and Delitzsch prefer the second alternative, holding that it happened while the chest was being carried up, no doubt when it had reached the court and was set down there for a time either within the hall or in front of it.

The placing under the wings is described plainly and then made to yield an inference. After the sacrificing ended, those same commentators say, the priests bore it to its room, into the hinder part of the house, under the outspread figures; Gill adds that the spot had been destined for it and answered to what it occupied in the earlier tabernacle, the wings reaching across the most holy place from wall to wall. From the detail that the shade fell over the poles too, they draw a conclusion about how it stood: if those great wings covered these as well, the chest was probably set so that its staves ran north and south rather than east and west — correcting, as they acknowledge, the way they had themselves sketched the arrangement elsewhere.

A small grammatical quarrel follows, and both these writers stand on one side of it. The clause, on their reading, means that the staves were long, so long that their heads could be seen from the Holy Place before the hinder room while remaining invisible outside; and they refuse the alternative version, that somebody had lengthened them, from which one interpreter inferred that new and longer ones had been made for the occasion. The tense cannot be a pluperfect in this connection, they argue, and on that alternative an object would have been marked by the usual particle; the verb stands intransitively, meaning to be long, literally to show length. Gill rejects the same opinion on other grounds, that nothing larger than what Moses had was required because the chamber was larger; and he rejects the opposite error too, that the staves were withdrawn altogether and laid aside now that a fixed station had been found and no further journey was in prospect, which would have been contrary to the command. They were drawn out, he concludes, only some little way.

Clarke takes the closing phrase for evidence about the book rather than about the furniture: the words that they are there unto this day prove the account was composed before the first temple fell, though how long before nobody can tell.
9:
The emphasis on what the ark did not contain is what the witnesses notice first. Ellicott calls it remarkable, and thinks it intended to make clear that the various things laid up before the testimony — the pot of manna, the rod, the copy of the Law — were not in the ark but, as in the last case is actually stated, at the side of it. Keil and Delitzsch give the remark a different purpose, simply to show that the law which enjoined that the ark should preserve the stone tables and nothing else had not been departed from in the lapse of time; and they note that Horeb is used here as the general name for the place where the law was given, instead of the more definite name. Gill reads the exclusion more narrowly still, that there were no other writings, or as one rabbi has it no other part of the law but the decalogue.

Gill will not let the exclusion settle the older question, and offers a grammatical escape from it. He grants that another account places the rod and the pot of manna in the ark, and answers that the particle rendered there may equally be rendered at, or with, or by, so that they might have stood not within it but in some place on the sides of it. Ellicott meets the same difficulty head on and decides it the other way, holding that unless some change afterwards took place, which is highly improbable, this clear statement must determine the interpretation of the well-known passage in the Epistle; no stress need be laid, he says, on the literal accuracy of the word wherein, since the purpose of that passage is simply a general description of the temple, its chief parts and its most sacred furniture.

What it means that these particular objects were the ones enshrined draws the longest reflection in the chapter, and it is Ellicott's. There is something singularly impressive, he writes, in the especial hallowing of the granite tables of the Law of Righteousness as the most sacred of all the revelations of the nature of God, since it binds religion and morality indissolubly together. It shows that God is best known to man not in his omnipotence, nor even in his infinite wisdom, which man can imitate only in slight degree, but in his moral nature, as the very Truth and Righteousness of which all that in man is called true and righteous is but the reflection. The one main object of all prophetic teaching, he adds, was to bring out the truth here implied, writing the law on the heart and on the mind and rebuking moral evil at least as strongly as religious error and apostasy.
10:
The cloud is read by every witness against the same precedent. Keil and Delitzsch set the two occasions side by side: at the dedication of the tabernacle the glory within the cloud filled the sanctuary so that Moses could not enter, and so it was now, the signification being identical, since that visible symbol of the gracious presence of God covered the house as a sign that the covenant-God had entered it and chosen it for the scene of his manifestation in Israel. Clarke measures how far it reached, holding that it appears to have filled not merely the holy of holies but the whole building, court and all, and to have become evident to the people, so that by this Solomon knew his place had been honoured and taken for a habitation.

A misreading the sequence invites is then corrected. By the inability of the ministers to stand we are not to understand that they were driven out, since the vapour did not descend until after they had come away; the words mean only that they could not remain in the Holy Place to perform their service, say to offer incense upon the altar. Clarke fixes the same moment, after the ark had been carried into the inner chamber and before any sacred office had yet begun.

Why they could not stand is answered three ways by Gill and a fourth by Ellicott. Gill offers the darkness first caused, or the light that broke out of it and dazzled them, or the terror struck into their minds, and notes that they could minister neither by burning incense, nor in the innermost room, where none but the high priest went and he on one day only, nor at the altar outside. Ellicott declines the word terror. They shrank, he says, from a glory which none could see and live, as the prophet felt undone when he beheld it in this very house and as even the Apostles trembled on entering the bright overshadowing and knew not what they said; yet it was not so much dread of a consuming fire as simple awe and reverence before an unspeakable splendour.

He then carries the symbol forward and back. That brightness, at once vapour and flame, had marked the divine presence on Sinai and had hallowed the consecration of the tabernacle, and now settled on the new building as a sign of its acceptance; in the visions of the prophet the same radiance is seen first filling the sanctuary and afterwards departing from it as polluted by manifold idolatry, while its return to the restored courts is solemnly promised with distinct reference to the coming of the Messiah, and with the declaration that it shall exceed what Solomon knew in all his magnificence. The sign clearly implies, he adds, a revelation of divine glory as it is seen not in the unveiled brightness of heaven but through a mystery, which is how it must always be seen on earth. Gill supplies from the other account what was happening outside at that moment, the Levites of the families of Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun arrayed in fine linen with their instruments at the east end of the altar, and a hundred and twenty trumpeters praising the Lord together with one sound.
12:
Solomon is speaking to frightened men, and both Gill and Henry say so before they say anything else. Gill has him perceive by the symbol that the Lord was come into his house to take up his dwelling in it, and, seeing the priests and people in consternation at it, speak these words to their comfort. Henry describes the same consternation and compares it with a later one, that the disciples of Christ feared when they entered into the cloud although it was a bright cloud, and so did the priests when they found themselves wrapped in a thick one. To silence their fears, Henry says, Solomon reminds them of what they could not but know, that the cloud is a token of God's presence and so far from being a mark of his displeasure that it is an indication of his favour, since he had himself said that he would appear in a cloud. Clarke supplies the two precedents, the cloud by which God showed himself present with Israel in the wilderness and the cloud at the dedication of the tabernacle.

That God should dwell in darkness is then turned into doctrine. Henry states the paradox without softening it: God is light and dwells in light, but he dwells with men in the thick darkness and makes that his pavilion, because they could not bear the dazzling brightness of his glory, so that thus our holy faith is exercised and our holy fear increased, whereas where God dwells in light faith is swallowed up in vision and fear in love. He adds the rule that carried him there, that nothing is more effectual to reconcile us to dark dispensations than to consider what God hath said and to compare his word and works together. Ellicott makes the same point as a matter of optics: the description of the cloud as thick darkness in no way contradicts the idea of the glory shining through it, for human eyes are easily darkened by excess of light, and this mingled light and darkness symbolises, perhaps more strikingly than even the literal darkness of the Most Holy Place, the mystery which veils a presence known to be infinitely glorious but in its nature incomprehensible.

A conjecture on the text is reported here and refused. Ellicott notes that one scholar, on the strength of a single Chaldee version, would correct thick darkness to Jerusalem, urging that the reading harmonises better with the verse about choosing a city, that the promise of the Psalm stands closely connected there with the great promise to David, that Solomon would naturally cite it, and that his whole utterance gains in simplicity. The suggestion is ingenious, Ellicott answers, but it lacks authority both external and internal. The Greek of one manuscript and the Latin agree with the Hebrew text, and Josephus, though he gives a verbose paraphrase of the prayer, evidently had the received reading before him, since he contrasts the mystery and ubiquity of the divine presence with the material shrine. Nor is it easy to conceive how, from a passage as simple and prosaic as this would be with the other reading, the more difficult but far more striking reading of the present text could have arisen.
13:
The address changes direction at this point, and Gill marks the turn: having quieted the priests and people with a few words, Solomon faced about and spoke to the Lord. Clarke reads the sentence as a statement of certainty rather than of achievement, that the king was now fully convinced the thing pleased God and that a settled habitation had been taken. Henry dramatises it as a legal act, a formal giving of possession: God by the cloud had come down to claim it, and Solomon in a few words solemnly makes the conveyance — the building entirely his own, raised and furnished for him, a dwelling to abide in for ever, never to be alienated nor turned to any other use, and the ark never to be removed again. It is the king's joy, Henry adds, that the owner has entered, and his desire that he should keep what he holds.

The posture he spoke from is filled in from the parallel account. Gill has him standing before the altar with his face toward it and toward the inner rooms filled with the cloud, and then turning so that the altar lay behind him while he looked out over the assembled people. Ellicott adds what the other record supplies, a brasen scaffold three cubits high in the midst of the court, from which he could turn alternately toward the sanctuary and toward the crowd outside. Clarke observes that the words of the benediction are nowhere stated, and supposes them to have been those the high priest pronounced, since Solomon seems here to act that part; though he thinks the model may rather have been Moses, who blessed Israel when he saw the tabernacle finished as commanded, or David, who did the like once the ark had reached his city and the offerings were complete.

The blessing itself recites a promise kept, and the text of it is disputed. Keil and Delitzsch note that the undertaking to choose a city and to raise David as prince is taken freely from the older book rather than quoted, and that the other record inserts before the choice of David a clause about choosing Jerusalem that the name might be there, so that the affirmation answers more precisely to the denial preceding it, whereas the middle term drops out here. Ellicott holds the gap needs repairing for coherence of idea and would restore the fuller wording, drawing out a double parallel: as there had been temporary resting places, Gilgal and Shiloh and Kirjathjearim and Zion, so rulers had been raised up in succession and removed again, and now one fixed sanctuary was to answer to one royal line continuing for ever. Clarke reports the same restoration from another scholar, who counts thirteen Hebrew words lost from this book and happily preserved in the other; but he does not think they ever belonged here, since no version of this passage carries them, and says only that their presence elsewhere helps complete the sense. Gill contributes the arithmetic, that the exodus was by now about four hundred and eighty-eight years past.
17:
David's intention is reported in order to be approved, and Keil and Delitzsch note how carefully the commendation is worded. The account of that design, and of the answer that a son should execute the work, is copied from the older book only so far as this, that the intention is praised as such: thou didst well that it was in thy mind. Gill describes it in three degrees, that the mind was disposed toward the project, the heart set upon it, and a resolution taken up; and he supplies the channel by which the refusal arrived, a message delivered through Nathan the prophet.

What follows is a claim that the promise has been performed, and the same pair read it as unpacking a phrase used a little earlier. When Solomon says the Lord has established what he spoke, he is unfolding his own earlier remark that what the mouth uttered the hand fulfilled: the throne of David had been made over to him, the fabric raised, and a chamber prepared within it for the ark of the covenant. From that sequence they draw a judgement about the whole building, which is thereby declared to have the chest for its kernel and star, since it served as the seat of the glory of God. Gill keeps the reference narrow, taking the performed promise for what had been said to David about his son's undertaking, and identifying the prepared chamber as the most holy place.

That the ark is said to hold the covenant rather than the tables is what the last two witnesses stop on. Clarke reasons from the earlier verse: since nothing lay inside but the two stones, those stones are what is here called the covenant, that is, a sign of it — as our Lord calls the cup the new covenant in his blood, meaning the sign of it, since to say this is my body is to say this is the emblem of my body.

Ellicott takes the same usage as a window on what a divine covenant is, and defines it against the human kind. Such compacts are not, like most between men, undertakings of reciprocal engagements between parties regarded as independent; that conception of the relation between God and his creatures he calls monstrous. They proceed simply from the divine will, expressed in a summons addressed to an individual or a nation; they begin in free grace and blessing, and ask only that those addressed should believe what is offered and act in obedience to that belief. He finds the order stated in the Decalogue itself, which opens not with a demand but with a description of deliverance out of the house of bondage, the mercy that constituted Israel afresh as a peculiar people; and it is on the ground of that rescue, rather than of omnipotence as Creator and Sustainer of the world, that the commandments are urged, becoming thereby the words of the covenant. The Apostle proceeds the same way, he adds, when he calls Christians to absolute self-devotion and appeals to them by the mercies of God.
22:
That the king prayed it himself is the first thing Henry finds remarkable. Solomon did not appoint one of the priests to do it, nor one of the prophets, but did it himself in the presence of all the congregation. It was well that he was able to, Henry says, a sign that he had improved the pious education his parents gave him; with all his learning he had learnt to pray, and knew how to express himself to God suitably on the spur of the occasion and without a prescribed form, so that in the crowd of his philosophical transactions, his proverbs and his songs, he did not forget his devotions. It was well too that he was willing, and not shy of performing divine service before so great a congregation, being far from thinking it a disparagement to be his own chaplain and the mouth of the assembly to God — and shall any think themselves too great, Henry asks, for that office in their own families? Solomon in all his other glory, even on his ivory throne, looked not so great as he did now.

Where he stood is given from this account and the other together. Gill places him at the altar of burnt offering in the court of the priests, and takes the altar itself to be typical of Christ, who is always to be in sight in prayer and through whom all sacrifices of prayer and praise become acceptable; and from the parallel he adds the scaffold of brass, five cubits long and five broad and three high, in the midst of the court, a sort of pulpit, round as a laver, on which the king kneeled. Clarke gives the same scaffold and action, that Solomon ascended it and kneeled down with his hands spread up to heaven. Henry reads the position itself as a claim: he stood before the altar, intimating that he expected the success of his prayer in virtue of that sacrifice which should be offered up in the fulness of time and was typified by the sacrifices offered there.

The two postures are then defended separately. Of the kneeling Henry observes that it is only established from the later verse where Solomon is said to rise from his knees, that it is the most proper posture for prayer, and that the greatest of men must not think it below them to kneel before the Lord their Maker — quoting a poet of his own century to the effect that kneeling never spoiled silk stocking. Of the spread hands he says Solomon kept them so to the end, expressing his desire towards and expectation from God as a Father in heaven, offering the prayer from an open enlarged heart and at the same time reaching out with both arms to receive the mercy he prayed for; and he insists that such outward expressions of the fervour of devotion ought not to be despised or ridiculed.

Clarke answers the same point by showing how common the gesture was. It was a usual custom in all nations, he says: in prayer the hands were stretched out to heaven as if to invite and receive assistance from thence, while the suppliant, humbly kneeling, seemed to acknowledge at once his dependence and his unworthiness. He collects the instances from the Psalms, where the worshipper lifts his hands toward the holy oracle and is bidden lift them in the sanctuary and bless the Lord, and then from the heathen poets, one of whom has a man raise his hands, freed from their bonds, to the stars and call the eternal fires to witness, and another a suppliant on his knees turning about a silent face as though his arms were outstretched. So universal were these forms, Clarke concludes, that one of the heathens could say that all men in praying lift up their hands to heaven.
23:
The prayer opens by stating a ground, and Keil and Delitzsch explain what the ground is for. By granting the blessing promised to his people, the Lord has hitherto proved himself the true and only God in heaven and on earth, who keepeth covenant and mercy with those who walk before him with all their heart; and this acknowledgement, they say, provides the requisite confidence for offering a prayer which is sure of an answer. Gill puts the contrast more narrowly, that he is addressed as their covenant God and Father, and so distinguished from all the gods of the Gentiles.

Ellicott hears in the formula the record of a long education. The words are often used in the Psalms and stand especially in David's thanksgiving after the great promise, and they are evidently suggested by older utterances of devotion, as in the first recorded song at the Red Sea; in them, he says, we trace the process by which the Israelites were trained from the polytheism of their forefathers to the knowledge of the One only God. He is known to them first in the close personal relation of the God of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, to whom none is like of all the gods others worshipped; next in his universal relation to the universe, as God Almighty and Judge of the whole earth; and lastly, by the very meaning of his name, as the One Self-existent Being and source of all other life. Thus in the thanksgiving of David the higher belief is added at once to the comparison, and in this prayer the comparison is followed at once by the striking confession that the heaven of heavens cannot contain him.

The second half of the formula draws a point about what a covenant includes. Ellicott traces the phrase about keeping covenant and mercy to the close of the Second Commandment and to the revelation of God to Moses in the Mount, and calls it notable not merely because it describes God as manifesting himself most chiefly by showing mercy, but because it declares that mercy to be pledged to man as a chief part of his covenant — as it is afterwards said that to those who claim his covenant in Christ he is faithful and just to forgive sins. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same conclusion from the history rather than the wording, that the promise given to David, the beginning of whose fulfilment now lay before their eyes, was an emanation from the covenant faithfulness of God.

What Solomon then asks for is a promise he quotes in its conditional form, and both commentators notice what that leaves out. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the petition never to let a successor be wanting to David is put in the same conditional shape in which David had uttered the hope and in which the Lord had renewed the promise during the building, and that the wording here makes the divine rejection more distinctly a possibility; they add that the last of these verses is not a mere repetition of the one before it, as one commentator supposes, but the introduction to all the petitions that follow, reaching back to the whole promise rather than to the clause about the throne alone. Ellicott says outright what the quotation omits: the larger part of the promise extends beyond Solomon's citation of it, since it expressly declares that even if the seed of David fall away they shall be chastised but not cast off, a declaration which the prophet and the Psalmist both enforce by comparing the certainty of its fulfilment with the fixity of the ordinances of the sun and moon. Like the ordinary dispensations of Providence, he concludes, it is in itself fixed and immutable, though the actual enjoyment of its blessing by each individual or each age is conditional on right reception of it.
27:
The question is read as an exclamation, and both Gill and Clarke say what kind. Gill turns it into a series of his own: is it true, can any credit be given to it, who could ever have thought that so great and glorious a Being, who inhabits eternity and dwells in the highest heavens, should ever condescend to dwell on earth? Clarke calls the expression full of astonishment, veneration and delight, and locates the astonishment precisely — Solomon is struck with the immensity and dignity and grandeur of the divine Being, but especially with his condescension to dwell with men, so that although he sees by the filling of the place that God has come to make his abode with them, he still cannot help asking how such a God can dwell in such a place and with such creatures. Gill suspects a further reference, that Solomon may have had in view the condescension of the Son of God to tabernacle in human nature, his temple being the figure of that body in which the Godhead dwells.

Clarke then takes the plural forms as an invitation to astronomy, and accepts it at length. The words are all plural in the Hebrew, the heavens and the heavens of heavens; and what they imply, he says, is that there are systems, and systems of systems, each possessing its sun and its primary and secondary planets, all extending beyond each other in unlimited space in the same regular and graduated order we find prevailing in our own — which, for all its thousands of millions of miles in diameter, may be to some others no more than the area of the lunar orbit is to that of the furthest planet in ours. From that he draws two consequences. Suns, the centres of systems, may have been created at so immense a distance that their light has not yet reached this earth, though travelling at a hundred and ninety thousand miles every second, upwards of a million times swifter than the motion of a cannon ball. And had God created a system like ours every six days since the foundation of the world, keeping every seventh as a sabbath, the three hundred thousand and more systems so made would occupy but a speck in the inconceivable immensity of space.

Keil and Delitzsch are less interested in the immensity than in what the sentence is doing inside a prayer. The verses are closely connected in this sense, they say: keep thy words that were spoken to David, for although this temple cannot hold thine infinite divine nature, I know that thou wilt have respect to the prayer of thy servant and keep thine eyes open over this house. The clause about the heaven of heavens is therefore an intermediate thought, with which Solomon meets certain contracted ideas of the gracious presence of God in the temple. On that reading they reject two rival constructions of the connecting particle, that it means but or nevertheless and that it means as; and they reject with them the assertion that a new section of the prayer begins here, which they say rests on an inadmissible rendering of the verb that follows.
28:
The petition is offered in the character of a servant, and Gill marks the title. Solomon means himself, who though a king acknowledged himself, and esteemed it an honour to be, the servant of the Lord, and who was besides an humble suppliant. Keil and Delitzsch gloss the request that the divine eyes be open upon the house as a prayer that they be directed there by a special providence, and note that the words about night and day make the watching continual.

The ground of that request is found inside the verse itself. The same commentators point to the following clause, about the place where the name was promised to dwell, and say it carries within itself the reason the prayer rests on: because that name will be present, that is, because a gracious presence will be manifested there, the watching will also be kept up, so that a petition offered toward the spot may be heard. Clarke unfolds the clause into its effects, that power and glory will be shown forth in enlightening, quickening, pardoning, sanctifying and saving all sincere worshippers. Gill adds that eyes open toward the building mean eyes open toward the people praying in it, and that the site would see some displays of presence, power and providence, of goodness, grace and mercy.

Why the prayer should be offered toward the place rather than inside it is answered practically by one witness and doctrinally by two. Keil and Delitzsch observe simply that the phrase is used because the king himself stood in the court, facing the sanctuary. Clarke makes the direction a figure of mediation: both tabernacle and temple were types of our Lord, of God manifested in the flesh, who was and is the Mediator between God and man, so that all prayer, to be acceptable and entitled to a hearing, must pass through him, the human nature of Christ being the shrine in which dwelt all the fulness of the Godhead bodily. Gill says as much in his own terms, that Solomon asks not only for himself but for Israel then and in all succeeding ages, whenever they should look toward this spot and toward him whom it typified, since acceptance with God is to be ascribed to the blood and righteousness and sacrifice and mediation of another. Clarke takes the closing words of the petition, that God should hear in heaven his dwelling place and, hearing, forgive, for the true sense and doctrine of the whole.
31:
Clarke supplies the frame the rest of the prayer hangs on: Solomon puts here seven cases, in all of which the mercy and intervention of God would be indispensably requisite, and he earnestly bespeaks that mercy on condition that the people pray towards that holy place and with a feeling heart make earnest supplication. The first, Clarke says, is a case of doubtfulness. Where a man has sustained an injury and charges it upon a suspected person without being able to bring direct evidence of the fact, the accused is permitted to come before the altar of God and purge himself by his personal oath; and Solomon prays that God may not permit a false oath to be taken, but will discover the truth, so that the wicked shall be condemned and the righteous justified. Gill fills in the kind of wrong meant, an unfaithfulness in a trust committed to him or the like, and notes that the hearing in heaven is asked when the injured person makes supplication to have justice done him.

The second case is defeat, and here the confession asked for is specific. Clarke describes enemies making inroads and defeating them in battle and leading them into captivity, because God, displeased with their transgressions, has delivered them up; and then the turning again, and the confessing of the name of God, which they had in effect denied either by neglecting his worship or by becoming idolatrous, before the petition that they may be brought again to the land. Gill fills in the picture — beaten and routed, many slain and others carried captive, which had been their case and might well be again, though this was now a time of peace — and marks what kind of sin is to be forgiven, not personal but public sin, which would be the cause of such a calamity. Keil and Delitzsch anchor the petition in the law, noting that it answers to the threatenings under which the nation is warned that it shall be smitten before its enemies.

The third case is drought, and it yields the one grammatical dispute in this stretch of the prayer. Clarke describes God refusing the early and the latter rain because of their sin and their ceasing to walk in the good way, so that the appointed weeks of harvest come in vain, there being no crop. Gill notes that heaven may be said to be shut up when the air is quite serene and not a cloud in it, and that the forgiveness asked for is a removing of the judgment. Keil and Delitzsch settle two clauses against rival renderings, the first meaning because thou humblest them rather than that thou hearest them, the second because thou teachest them the good way; and they show why the point matters. The two clauses correspond to one another and together contain a motive for forgiveness: because God teaches his people and seeks by chastisement to bring them back to the good way when they fail to keep his commandments, he must forgive when they recognise the punishment as a divine chastisement and come to him with penitential prayer.
37:
The fourth case is a list rather than a single trouble, and Keil and Delitzsch run through it with the law open beside them. It relates to the removal of other land-plagues: famine, pestilence, blight and mildew in the corn, locusts, oppression by enemies within their own territory, and lastly plagues and diseases of every kind, each of them threatened against the rebellious in the older books. They notice one small stylistic touch, that the word for the devourer is joined to the word for the locust without a connecting particle, which they take to be a way of depicting the plague more vividly before the eyes of the hearers. Gill adds a memory that would have made the first item concrete, that there had been a three years' famine in the time of David and might be again, for all that the land was one flowing with milk and honey.

Clarke breaks the same list into nine heads and defines each. Famine is a scarcity or total want of bread, springing necessarily from the drought just mentioned; pestilence is any general and contagious disease; blasting is anything by which the crops are injured so that the ear is never matured, but instead of wholesome grain there is a black offensive dust; mildew is whatever vitiates or corrodes the texture of the stalk, destroys the flowers and blossoms, or causes the young fruits to fall from their stems. The locust he calls a well-known curse in the East, a species of grasshopper that multiplies by millions and covers the face of the earth for many miles square, leaving neither herb nor grass upon the ground nor leaf nor bark upon the trees; the caterpillar he takes for the same creature in its young state, the one term referring to locusts brought by winds from other countries and the other to those bred in the land itself. The remaining heads are an enemy attacking their defenced cities, which he calls the keys and barriers of the land; any other plague affecting the surface of the body; and sickness, whatever impaired the strength or disturbed the natural functions.

What makes such prayers acceptable is then located inside the man rather than in his circumstances. Clarke holds that all these cases were to be brought before the Lord by persons having a deep sense of the wickedness which induced God so to afflict them, and that only those who knew the plague of their own hearts — the deep-rooted moral corruption of their nature and the destructive sinfulness of sin — were likely to pray in such a manner at all. Gill keeps the clause wide, covering any prayer on account of any of these things or of any other; and on the phrase about God hearing in his dwelling place he cannot resist the comparison, that heaven was more properly his dwelling place than the house Solomon had built and the Lord had just taken possession of. The end of the whole petition Gill reads as gratitude rather than dread, that they may fear him for his goodness' sake in hearing their prayer, removing their affliction and bestowing his blessings upon them, and particularly in forgiving their sins.
41:
Who the stranger is gets three descriptions that differ in emphasis. Gill makes him one of another country, belonging to none of the tribes of Israel, yet having some knowledge of and disposition toward the true worship of God. Clarke reads this fifth case as relating to heathens who arrive from abroad meaning to become proselytes, that they might be received and blessed and protected as the native-born were, so that the name of God should be known over the face of the earth. Keil and Delitzsch point out that Solomon assumes as certain that foreigners will come and worship before the Lord in this house, and they recall that Moses himself had allowed those living among the Israelites to offer sacrifice.

The verse about what such a visitor will have heard is read by the same pair as a parenthesis rather than a fresh clause, inserted to explain the phrase about coming for the sake of the name, with the main thought resumed afterwards at the words about coming and praying. They observe that the strong hand and the outstretched arm are joined together as a standing expression for the wondrous manifestations of divine omnipotence in the guidance of Israel. Gill expands the great name into its contents, the title by which God is known as the eternal, immutable and self-existent Being, together with the perfections of his nature as displayed in his mighty works.

The closing phrase about the house being called by that name is where Keil and Delitzsch correct the usual readings. They trace the expression to an older passage from which it has been taken and transferred here, and argue from the original that the common explanations are erroneous — neither that the building is named after him, nor that his name is invoked over it at its dedication. The name of the Lord, they say, always denotes in the Scriptures his working among his people or in his kingdom; and pronouncing it over a nation or over a sanctuary presupposes that working within it, and amounts to a confession and acknowledgment of it. The reason given for hearing the foreigner is of a piece with this, that all the peoples of the earth may know him and fear him as his own do.
44:
Keil and Delitzsch set out the architecture of the two petitions that close the prayer. Solomon finally asks that when prayers are directed towards the temple by those who are far away from both the city and the house, they may be heard; the sixth case is Israel engaged in war with an enemy by the appointment of God, and the seventh is Israel carried away by enemies on account of its sins. They also defend the passage against a commentator who argued on doctrinal grounds that these verses are an interpolated addition, agreeing rather with the answer already made to him: it is quite in harmony with the original plan that the two cases should be anticipated in which the prayers of Israelites at a distance from the seat of the sanctuary are directed towards it.

Clarke fastens on the qualifying clause and makes it the whole of the case. The sixth petition refers to wars undertaken by divine appointment — whithersoever thou shalt send them — because in no other wars could they expect the blessing and concurrence of the Lord, and in no other could the God of truth and justice maintain their cause. He then presses the limitation forward into his own day, and refuses to let it be transferred. There were such wars under the Mosaic dispensation; there are none such under the Christian, nor can there be any, since the Son of man is come not to destroy men's lives but to save them. Except mere defensive war, he says, all others are diabolic; and he ends with a question rather than a qualification, asking whether, if there were no provocations, there would be any attacks at all, and consequently any need of defensive wars.

Gill keeps to the circumstances that would make such a war lawful in the first place, describing an enemy in a foreign country threatening to invade them, or having trespassed on their borders, or in some other way infringed their liberties and privileges, and so having given them just occasion to go to war; and he reads the petition that follows as a prayer for success, while the clause about maintaining their cause, in Keil and Delitzsch's rendering, asks God to take up the case as his own.
46:
What kind of sin the seventh case supposes is inferred by Clarke from its punishment. It must refer to some general defection from truth, to some species of false worship or idolatry or corruption of the ordinances of the Most High, since for it the people are here stated to be delivered into enemy hands and carried away captive, which was the standing penalty for idolatry and is described in the next verse as acting perversely and committing wickedness. Gill reads the opening clause more narrowly still, of the very persons who had gone forth to battle in the case before, not observing the divine commands as they ought.

Clarke then quarrels with the received translation of the parenthesis, and on a point of logic. As it stands, he says, the second clause renders the supposition in the first entirely nugatory, for if there be no man that sinneth not, it is useless to say if they sin. The contradiction is removed by reference to the original, which should be rendered should they sin against thee, for there is no man that may not sin — that is, nobody is impeccable, nobody infallible, nobody incapable of transgressing. He observes that the translators themselves understood the word so elsewhere, since earlier in this very chapter they render it if a man trespass, which certainly implies that he might or might not do so, and that they do the like in several other places; the Hebrew, he adds, has no separate form for expressing words in a permissive sense.

The turning that follows is described by Gill in two stages and corrected by Keil and Delitzsch in one particular. Gill takes the first phrase for a returning to their own heart, a remembering of the offences that had caused the captivity and a reflecting upon them, and the second for a coming back to God in the most sincere and cordial manner, with great ingenuity and uprightness. The other pair refuse the rendering that would make the first phrase mean they feel remorse, on the ground that the form used cannot carry that reflexive sense; what is meant is that they take the matter to heart. They also widen the scope of the petition: Solomon had in view the threat of the law about being scattered among the nations, but does not confine himself to the exile of a whole people foretold there, extending the request rather to every case of transportation into hostile territory. The words of the confession itself, they note, were the very ones afterwards adopted by those actually in captivity.
50:
What Solomon asks for the captives is less than might be expected, and Clarke says so plainly: he does not pray that they may be delivered out of that captivity, but that their enemies may use them well, and that they may, as formerly, be kept a separate and distinct people. Keil and Delitzsch give the clause in its literal form, make them for compassion before their captors, that these may have compassion upon them — that is, cause them to meet with compassion from the enemies who have carried them away. Gill reads the forgiveness asked for in the previous clause as one that would show itself in a return, since by bringing them back to their own land it would appear that the Lord had forgiven their trespasses.

Ellicott traces what became of the petition, and finds it answered unevenly. The prayer was singularly fulfilled at the captivity of Judah in Babylon, though we hear of no such thing in relation to the captivity of the lost tribes in Assyria. He points to the exceptional favour shown by Nebuchadnezzar, and by the king of the Book of Esther, to the Jews in Babylon, and still more to the greater boon of restoration granted them by Cyrus and Darius and by the king of the Book of Nehemiah; and he adds that, like the whole course of the fortunes of the Jews in their subsequent dispersion, these things, however they may be accounted for, are certainly unique in history.

The ground on which the whole prayer rests is stated last, and Gill unfolds each of its terms. They are God's people and his inheritance because he had chosen them above all people to be a special people to him, and to be his portion and possession; Keil and Delitzsch add the image the verse itself supplies, that he brought them out of Egypt from the midst of the furnace of iron. The request that his eyes be open Gill takes to mean attentive, and extends beyond the moment, covering not only Solomon's present supplication but any other he should hereafter put up in this place. And the separation named in the last verse he resolves into four acts: God separated them by his choice of them in his own mind, by the redemption of them out of Egypt, by the peculiar laws he gave them, and by the special blessings he conferred upon them.
54:
Henry marks the shape of what follows before he takes up its content. After the sermon in one of his books Solomon gives us the conclusion of the whole matter, and so he does here at the end of this long prayer; the act is called blessing the people, and he performed it standing, that he might be the better heard and because he blessed as one having authority. Never were words more fitly spoken, Henry says, nor more pertinently, and never was a congregation dismissed with anything more likely to affect them and abide with them. Gill reads the moment typically, that in interceding for his people before the altar the king was a figure of Christ, and notes that the benediction was pronounced with a loud voice. Keil and Delitzsch add a small point of construction, that the clause about his hands being spread toward heaven is circumstantial and belongs with what precedes, so that the sense is not of a gesture made afterwards but of a man rising from his knees with them already lifted.

Whether what he uttered was a blessing at all is a question Ellicott raises and half answers. To bless the congregation was the special duty and privilege of the priests, and yet throughout this whole narrative the king, and the king alone, is conspicuous. It is to be noted, however, he adds, that the words here are not strictly of benediction but rather of praise and prayer to God and of exhortation to those listening. Gill describes the same double office without feeling the difficulty, having Solomon turn from the altar to face the crowd and deliver his farewell not only as father of his people but as preacher in Jerusalem, closing with a word of admonition. Clarke states flatly where the blessing proper is to be found, in the two verses that follow.

Ellicott also notes what this account leaves out at exactly this juncture, that the parallel record inserts a striking passage describing the kindling of the sacrifice by fire from heaven and, apparently, a second manifestation of the cloud of glory.
56:
What Solomon singles out for thanksgiving is what Henry finds worth dwelling on. He stood up to bless the congregation, Henry observes, but began with blessing God, for we must in everything give thanks; and the thing he blesses God for is not wealth or honour or power or victory, but rest, as if that were a blessing more valuable than any of those. Let not those who have rest undervalue that blessing, Henry adds, though they want some others. He also describes what the second half of the verse does with the promises: Solomon writes, as it were, a receipt in full on the back of the bonds, declaring that there has not failed one word of all God's good promises — a discharge given in the name of all Israel, to the everlasting honour of the divine faithfulness and the everlasting encouragement of all who build upon the divine promises.

Keil and Delitzsch locate the two halves of the praise in two different sets of promises, the first in the pledge of rest given in the law and its fulfilment recorded after the conquest, the second in the blessings promised to obedience. They then qualify the word rest historically: God had already given Israel rest by means of Joshua when the land was taken, but since many parts of it still remained in the hands of the Canaanites, that rest was only fully secured by David's victories over all their enemies.

Ellicott carries the same word forward and then turns it round. Now for the first time the frequent promise of rest, partially fulfilled after the conquest and again after the establishment of David's kingdom, was perfectly accomplished under Solomon the Peaceful, and the whole charter of gift of the promised land was for the first time thoroughly entered upon; and of that rest the transfer of the ark from the shifting tabernacle to the fixed temple was at once a sign and a pledge. Yet Solomon's own subsequent words imply that entering into the rest was conditional on Israel fulfilling its part of the covenant by walking in the ways of the Lord — a condition which he knew so well, and which he himself broke, and all Israel with him. Hence, Ellicott says, the fulfilment of the foreboding which emerges so constantly in his prayer, and hence the glory and happiness of his age proved but a gleam of prosperity, soon to be swallowed up in dissension and disaster.
57:
The first thing asked for after the thanksgiving is presence, and both Gill and Henry rate it above anything else that might have been requested. Gill fills in who the fathers were — Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, and those that came out of Egypt, and especially the generation that entered the land under Joshua and subdued it — and describes what such company had meant, to guide and direct them, to protect and defend them, to succeed and prosper them. Nothing is more desirable, he says, and Solomon could not have sought a greater blessing for himself or for those he governed. Henry counts it the first of four things the king desires for them, and calls it all in all to the happiness of a church and a nation.

What comes next is a change in the people rather than in their circumstances, and Gill takes the inclining of the heart for the work of the Spirit, bending them to love and fear and serve God and to attend upon his worship, his word and his ordinances.

Ellicott makes this clause, set beside the exhortation a few verses later, the occasion for stating what he takes to be the faith underlying the whole idea of covenant. It is a trust in the true though mysterious co-operation of preventing grace, which must be recognised in any adequate conception of God as the source of all life and action, physical and spiritual, with that free responsibility of man which is the ultimate truth of the inner human consciousness. The heart is inclined, and yet the heart must yield itself. That conviction grows deeper and plainer, he argues, in proportion as a man realises better the inward life of the soul as contrasted with the outward life of event and action, and realises accordingly a dominion exercised over the soul by grace, over and above the rule of providence in the visible world; which is why it emerges especially in the Psalms, the Proverbs and the prophetic books, and why through the great psalm of the Law the persuasion expresses itself again and again that only by gift can anyone be enabled to obey. Under the covenant of the Spirit the matter is brought out in all its fulness, he concludes, perhaps most vividly in the celebrated paradox that bids men work out their own salvation because it is God which worketh in them both to will and to do of his good pleasure.
59:
These verses are a postscript rather than part of the prayer proper, and Clarke says so before noting what is missing from them. This and the following verse are a sort of supplement to the prayer that ended earlier; but there is an important addition in the parallel place, which he quotes in full — the petition that the Lord God arise into his resting place, he and the ark of his strength, that his priests be clothed with salvation and his saints rejoice in goodness, and that he turn not away the face of his anointed but remember the mercies of David his servant. Keil and Delitzsch render the request itself closely: may these words, which Solomon has prayed, be near to the Lord day and night, that he may secure the right of his servant the king and of his people, as every day demands. They note that the words he refers to are the petitions already offered rather than anything new, so that the verse gathers up the whole prayer and asks that it stand before God continually.

The end proposed is not Israel's advantage but the world's knowledge, and Gill lists the ways such knowledge would come. All the people of the earth would learn that the Lord is God by his chastising the people of Israel when they sinned, by his hearing and answering their prayers, by his forgiving their sins and delivering them out of their troubles, and by his maintaining their cause and protecting them in the enjoyment of their blessings. On the clause that there is none else he is brief and absolute: no God besides him, all others being fictitious deities or nominal ones, while he only is the one living and true God.

The exhortation that closes the address is glossed by all three in nearly the same words. Keil and Delitzsch take the perfect heart to be one wholly and undividedly devoted to the Lord; Gill resolves it into sincerity in love to him, unitedness in worship of him and constancy in obedience to him; Clarke compresses it to two clauses, that they be sincere in their faith and irreproachable in their conduct.
62:
The scale of the offering draws an arithmetical objection and a careful answer. Keil and Delitzsch report that the thank-offering consisted, in accordance with the magnitude of the divine grace shown, of twenty-two thousand oxen and a hundred and twenty thousand sheep, and that one commentator has tried to set the figures aside as too large by calculating that, spread over seven sacrificial days of twelve hours, they would require about five oxen and twenty-five sheep to be offered every minute for the king alone. The calculation holds, they answer, only if its three assumptions do: that the whole number was for the king alone, that none but priests and Levites could slaughter and prepare, and that all the flesh was to be consumed upon the altar.

Henry does not dispute the figures but sets them beside two other occasions. The heathen thought themselves generous offering sacrifices by hundreds; Solomon outdid them and offered by thousands. When Moses dedicated his altar the peace-offerings were twenty-four bullocks and, of rams and goats and lambs, a hundred and eighty; then the people were poor, but now that they had increased in wealth more was expected of them, for where God sows plentifully he must reap accordingly. Henry adds the comparison that stings: thirty oxen a day served Solomon's own table, but thousands went to God's altar, and few are thus minded, to spend more upon their souls than upon their bodies. Gill and Clarke take the total to cover all fourteen days, and Clarke asks how they could possibly have disposed of the blood of so many victims.

Ellicott insists the real difficulty has been mislocated. The number can hardly be due to any error in the text, since it is exactly reproduced in the parallel account and by Josephus, and much explanation has been wasted through misunderstanding what is actually hard about it. That such a mass of victims could be brought or consumed is comparatively easy to conceive, given the vastness of the multitude assembled from the whole of Solomon's dominions; the real difficulty is to conceive how, even through the fourteen days and over the whole hallowed portion of the court, they could have been offered at all. His suggestion is that it might have been deemed sufficient actually to sacrifice only certain representative victims of each hundred and simply to dedicate the rest, leaving them to be killed and eaten elsewhere. He then turns the profusion into a warning: good as it was in expressing the natural desire of all to offer at such a time, it may have involved something of the idea so frequent in heathen sacrifice and so condemned by the prophets, that the Lord would be pleased with thousands of rams; and something of that display of the magnificence of king and people, even in the act of homage to God, which the history throughout seems to imply.

The hallowing of the court is explained alike by all: the brazen altar was too little, so its middle was set apart for the overflow, on altars of earth or stone raised for the purpose and taken down afterwards, as some think, or on bare ground, as others suppose. Henry draws the encouragement that those who will be generous in serving God need not stint themselves for want of room. Ellicott uses the same verse to make a point about the narrator rather than the ceremony: the idea that the king performed the priest's ministerial office is manifestly improbable, since he who brought a sacrifice was always said to offer it while the priest accepted it in the name of the Lord; but the absence of all mention of the priests, even in the hallowing of the court, is characteristic of the whole narrative, in which the king alone is prominent.
65:
The extent of the gathering is given by its two limits, and the limits are argued over. Keil and Delitzsch read the phrase as covering the whole land in its fullest extent from north to south, from the neighbourhood of Hamath to the brook of Egypt. Ellicott identifies the northern limit as the great valley between the two mountain ranges, which the Greeks knew by a name of their own, the main entrance to Palestine from the north, down which the hosts of Assyria and Babylon so constantly poured, and judges that at this time it extended beyond Damascus. On the southern limit he corrects a natural mistake: the river of Egypt is not the Nile nor any of its branches, since the word used signifies rather a brook or torrent, and the torrent described elsewhere as the border of Israel is identified by all authorities with the one falling into the sea at El-Arish. Clarke names both ends differently, taking the first for Antioch of Syria and the second for the Rhinocorura, but reaches the same conclusion, that the phrase means from one extremity of the land to the other.

What the king contributed to the feast Gill takes to be both his own portion and more besides: the parts of the peace offerings which belonged to him and were offered by way of thanksgiving on the occasion, together with whatever he might as a liberal prince provide for the entertainment. On the day of dismissal Gill is exact, and admits a small discrepancy: the eighth day is the eighth of the feast of tabernacles, a solemn day falling on the twenty-second of the month, at the close of which leave to depart was given, though by the other account they did not actually go until the twenty-third.

Clarke closes on the mood of the people and then on what became of it. They blessed the king, wishing him all spiritual and temporal happiness; they were contented with their king, at peace among themselves and happy in their God, so that they returned to their houses magnifying him for all his bounty to them, to their country and to their king. How happy these people must have been, Clarke writes, and how prosperous, had their king continued to walk uprightly before God — but the king fell, and the nation followed his example.
